course.title: Control Theory
course.description: How feedback makes machines hold a target: block diagrams, response shapes, PID, stability and tuning.
course.audience: Adults who have studied introductory calculus and mechanics. No Laplace transforms required.

paragraphs: A cruise control holds a car at a set speed by measuring the speed many times a second, comparing it with the setting, and opening or closing the throttle according to the difference, so a hill or a headwind is corrected without the driver touching anything. A thermostat, the autofocus of a camera and the autopilot of an aircraft work on the same principle, which is called feedback, and control theory is the study of how loops built on it behave and how to design them.

Feedback lets a machine hold its target while the machine itself wears and changes and while things outside push on it, which is why it is used so widely. A loop can also misbehave, by stopping short of its target, overshooting it or swinging back and forth with growing size, and each of these behaviours follows from a small number of equations. With them you can take a plant and a controller and say in advance how quickly the output will rise, how far it will overshoot, where it will settle and whether it will settle at all, and you can choose the controller's settings to meet a written requirement.
outcomes: You'll be able to reduce a feedback loop to one gain.
You'll be able to read and compute first and second order responses.
You'll be able to explain and tune P, I and D terms.
You'll be able to test a loop for stability.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Calculus: Change and Accumulation, Physics: Motion and Forces, Maths Foundations.

concepts.title: Loop parts
concepts.summary: A feedback loop has a plant, a sensor, a comparison with a target and a controller acting on the error.

concepts.title: Sensitivity
concepts.summary: Feedback shrinks the effect of plant changes and disturbances on the output, at the cost of loop gain being spent.

concepts.title: Combining blocks
concepts.summary: Blocks in series multiply; a feedback loop of forward gain G and feedback gain H gives G/(1+GH).

concepts.title: Sign convention
concepts.summary: Negative feedback subtracts the measurement at the summing junction.

concepts.title: Time constant
concepts.summary: The time for a first-order step response to cover 63.2 percent of the way to its final value.

concepts.title: Rate proportional to gap
concepts.summary: tau dy/dt = K u - y says the output closes the gap to its target at a rate proportional to the gap.

concepts.title: Closed-loop time constant
concepts.summary: tau_cl = tau/(1+K Kp): more gain makes it faster.

concepts.title: Steady-state error
concepts.summary: The final value is K Kp/(1+K Kp), always less than 1 for finite gain.

concepts.title: Damping ratio
concepts.summary: zeta = c/(2 sqrt(k m)): below 1 the response overshoots and rings; at 1 it is critical.

concepts.title: Overshoot
concepts.summary: Peak overshoot Mp = exp(-pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2)).

concepts.title: Time-domain specifications
concepts.summary: Rise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error describe a step response.

concepts.title: Damping from overshoot
concepts.summary: zeta = -ln(Mp) / sqrt(pi^2 + ln^2 Mp).

concepts.title: Proportional term
concepts.summary: u = Kp e: action proportional to the current error.

concepts.title: Steady-state error
concepts.summary: For a plant with DC gain G0, a unit step leaves e = 1/(1 + Kp G0).

concepts.title: Integral term
concepts.summary: Ki times the accumulated error, which keeps growing until the error is gone.

concepts.title: Windup
concepts.summary: When the actuator saturates the integral keeps growing and must be unwound later.

concepts.title: Derivative term
concepts.summary: Kd de/dt acts on the rate of change, damping approach before overshoot.

concepts.title: Noise amplification
concepts.summary: Derivative action multiplies high-frequency noise by 2 pi f.

concepts.title: Stable
concepts.summary: Every disturbance dies away: all characteristic roots have negative real parts.

concepts.title: Cubic test
concepts.summary: s^3 + a2 s^2 + a1 s + a0 is stable if all coefficients are positive and a2 a1 > a0.

concepts.title: Ultimate-gain method
concepts.summary: Raise Kp until steady oscillation; then P=0.5Ku, PI=0.45Ku, PID=0.6Ku, Ti=Tu/2, Td=Tu/8.

concepts.title: Reaction-curve method
concepts.summary: From a step test fit gain K, delay L and time constant T, then PID Kp=1.2T/(K L), Ti=2L, Td=0.5L.

concepts.title: Anti-windup
concepts.summary: Stop integrating while the output is saturated.

concepts.title: Feedforward
concepts.summary: Command the expected control from the setpoint so feedback only fixes the remainder.

lessons.title: Why close the loop

blocks.text: A toaster set for ninety seconds heats for ninety seconds, whether the slice is thin or thick and whether the kitchen is warm or cold, because nothing in it ever looks at the bread. A home thermostat works differently: it measures the room, compares the reading with the temperature on the dial, and switches the boiler according to the difference.
The difference matters as soon as the machine being controlled changes, as real machines do with wear, load and supply voltage.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the parts of a feedback loop, compare how open-loop and closed-loop controllers respond when the plant changes, and compute a closed-loop gain.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson builds on the loop drawn here and on the formula for its gain.

lead.text: The controller sends a command to the machine it controls and never learns what the machine did, which is how the toaster behaves, and an arrangement of this kind is called **open-loop** control. It is cheap, because it needs no measuring device, and it works well whenever the machine behaves the same way every time and nothing disturbs it.

The second view adds a path that carries a measurement of the output back to the front. The controller no longer works from a plan alone, because it subtracts the measurement from the target and acts on the difference, and since the signals now travel round a closed circuit the arrangement is called **feedback**, or **closed-loop**, control.

afterFigure.text: Open loop is not simply worse, since a thermometer would only make a toaster dearer, but it can respond only to what its designer expected.

lead.text: The machine being controlled is the **plant**, and the quantity we want to hold, such as a room temperature, is its output. The target value is the **setpoint**, and a **sensor** measures the output so that the circle in the figure can subtract the measurement from the setpoint, giving the **error**.

The **controller** turns the error into a command, and the command reaches the plant through an **actuator**, the part that actually pushes on it. Anything from outside the loop that pushes the output away from where it should be is a **disturbance**.

reveal.text: The throttle is the only part of this loop that acts on the engine. The sensor and the computer only carry information, so without the throttle the loop could measure and decide but could not change anything.

lead.text: Take a plant whose output is twice its input, so that its **gain** is 2, and suppose we want an output of 1.0 for a target of 1. An open-loop controller has to know the plant, so the designer measures the gain once and builds in the reciprocal: the controller multiplies the target by 0.5 and passes the result to the plant, and the output is 2 × 0.5 × 1 = 1.0, exactly as wanted.

afterFigure.text: The weakness is that the 0.5 is a memory of how the plant used to behave. The output changes by the same percentage as the gain, whatever that turns out to be.

reveal.text: A fall of 20 percent in the plant gain became a fall of 20 percent in the output, with nothing in the chain to resist it. The next screen shows what happens when the controller is given the measurement.

lead.text: Now close the loop around the same plant, using a controller that multiplies the error by a large gain K, say K = 8. Write r for the target and y for the output. The error is r − y, the controller turns it into K(r − y), and the plant multiplies that by G, so y = GK(r − y). Collecting the terms in y gives y(1 + KG) = KG r, and therefore y/r = KG/(1 + KG).
The product KG is called the **loop gain**, because it is the factor a signal picks up on one trip around the loop.

afterFigure.text: The figure plots the output for a target of 1 against the plant gain, for the open-loop controller and for the closed loop with K = 8. The open-loop line rises steeply, which is why a fall in G costs it so much. The closed-loop curve climbs quickly and then flattens near 1, so that between G = 1.6 and G = 2 it is almost level. When KG is large the 1 in the denominator matters little, and the output depends on the setpoint and hardly at all on G.

diagram.alt: A graph of output against plant gain from 0.4 to 3. The open-loop output is a straight line through 1.0 at gain 2 and 0.8 at gain 1.6. The closed-loop output with controller gain 8 is a curve that flattens near 1, at 0.941 for gain 2 and 0.928 for gain 1.6.
diagram.caption: Output for a target of 1. Between G = 1.6 and G = 2 the open-loop output drops by 0.2 and the closed-loop output by 0.013.

steps.headline: Find the closed-loop output for K = 8, first with G = 2 and then with G = 1.6.

workedSteps.text: The loop gain is K times G, which is 8 × 2.
The output for a target of 1 is KG divided by 1 + KG.
At G = 1.6 the loop gain is 8 × 1.6, and the same formula applies.
The two outputs can be compared as a percent change from the first.
The open-loop output lost 20 percent for the same change in G, so feedback reduced the effect about fourteen times. The target was 1, and 0.941 is still short of it.

reveal.text: More controller gain brings the output closer to the target without ever delivering all of it. The next example works this through for K = 12, and the screen after it explains why some error always remains.

steps.headline: Repeat the calculation with a larger controller gain, K = 12.

workedSteps.text: At G = 2 the loop gain is 12 × 2.
The output is KG divided by 1 + KG.
At G = 1.6 the loop gain is 12 × 1.6, and the same formula applies.
A larger K should make the output move less than the 1.45 percent it moved at K = 8.

lead.text: The shortfall can be read from the formula. The error is the target minus the output, 1 − KG/(1 + KG) = 1/(1 + KG), which shrinks as the loop gain grows and still cannot reach zero for any finite K. With K = 8 and G = 2 it is 1/17, about 5.9 percent of the target, and this is the price the loop paid. The same factor 1 + KG is what shrinks the effect of a change in G, since the closed-loop output moved about fourteen times less than the open-loop output did.
An open-loop controller would lose a quarter of its output for this change.

reveal.text: The same loop gain protects against a larger change in G just as it did against a smaller one, although the protection weakens as KG falls with G.

recap.keyIdea: An open-loop controller follows a plan and a feedback controller follows a measurement, and with loop gain KG the closed-loop gain is KG/(1 + KG), which moves far less than the plant gain does.

blocks.text: In a feedback loop a sensor returns the output, a junction subtracts it from the setpoint to give the error, and the controller acts on that error through an actuator. For K = 8 and G = 2 the output is 16/17, so a 20 percent fall in the plant gain became a fall of only 1.45 percent at the output.
The price is that 1/(1 + KG) of the target is always missing, so a finite loop gain leaves a finite error.

blocks.text: Here is a feedback loop written as two equations: e = r − y, which says that the error is the setpoint minus the output, and y = 10e, which says that a plant of gain 10 multiplies the error. Substituting the first into the second gives y = 10r − 10y, so y/r = 10/11, or 0.909, and that single number is the gain of the whole loop.

Engineers draw the same loop as a diagram, with a box for each part, an arrow for each signal and a circle where signals are added or subtracted, and a diagram of a dozen boxes can be reduced to one gain by a few rules for combining them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a block diagram, multiply blocks in series, add blocks in parallel, and reduce a feedback loop to a single gain.
intro.whyItMatters: Every loop in the rest of the course is reduced with the rules in this lesson.

lead.text: Arrows carry signals, and a **block** is a box that multiplies the signal entering it by a number written inside, its gain. A **summing junction** is a circle with a cross, which adds the signals that enter it or subtracts them, with the sign marked beside each arrow. A dot is a **branch point**, where one signal is copied unchanged onto two paths.

afterFigure.text: The junction in the middle row computes a minus b, and a branch point does not split a signal into halves, since both paths carry the full value.

diagram.alt: Three symbols of a block diagram. A box multiplies the signal passing through it by its gain G. A circle with a cross adds or subtracts the signals entering it, as a minus b. A dot splits one signal into two identical copies.

reveal.text: Blocks in series multiply, a rule that the next screen states and shows for parallel paths too.

lead.text: When one block feeds the next, as in the first view, each multiplies the signal that reaches it, so the pair acts as a single block whose gain is the product of the two: a signal of 1 becomes 2 and then 6. A chain of any length reduces in the same way.

In the second view the signal is branched into two paths that meet again at a summing junction. Each path works on the full signal, and the junction adds the results, so the pair acts as a single block whose gain is the *sum* of the two, here 2 + 3 = 5.

afterFigure.text: The test is how the signal travels: if it passes through one block after the other the gains multiply, and if it divides and rejoins the gains add.

reveal.text: Both paths received the full signal of 2, so the output is 2 times the combined gain of 4.5.

lead.text: Each block in the figure obeys a one-line equation. The junction subtracts the fed-back signal from the setpoint, so the error is e = r − Hy, and the forward block multiplies the error, so y = Ge. The output appears on both sides, and substituting the first equation into the second gives y = G(r − Hy), which is y = Gr − GHy.

Moving the term in y to the left side gives y(1 + GH) = Gr, and therefore y/r = G/(1 + GH). The product GH is the [[loop gain|The factor a signal picks up on one trip round the loop. Met in 'Why close the loop'.]] again, now with the feedback block counted in, and the 1 comes from the setpoint's own contribution to the error.

afterFigure.text: With H = 1 the formula is the KG/(1 + KG) of the previous lesson, so that result was a special case.

steps.headline: Reduce the loop with G = 10, first with H = 1 and then with H = 0.5.

workedSteps.text: With H = 1 the loop gain is G times H.
With negative feedback the closed-loop gain is G divided by 1 + GH.
With H = 0.5 the product is smaller, and the denominator changes with it.
Divide G by that denominator.
Halving H raised the gain, from 0.909 to 1.667, because less of the output is subtracted at the junction.

steps.headline: Reduce the loop with G = 4 and H = 0.5.

workedSteps.text: The loop gain is G times H.
The denominator is 1 + GH.
The closed-loop gain is G divided by that denominator.
The result lies between G/(1 + G) = 0.8 and the limit 1/H = 2.

reveal.text: Adding the feedback gives G/(1 − GH), here 0.5/0.5 = 1, which is the formula for positive feedback. The next screen says why the sign convention has to be checked at every junction.

lead.text: Only the sign of the term in y changes between the two cases: subtracting the feedback gives G/(1 + GH) and adding it gives G/(1 − GH). Negative feedback is the usual arrangement for control, and a plus sign in a diagram is worth stopping on, because with GH near 1 the denominator of the positive-feedback formula approaches zero and the output grows without limit.

For negative feedback the figure shows what a large G does. The gain G/(1 + GH) approaches 1/H, so with H = 1 it climbs towards 1 and with H = 0.5 towards 2. This is why H must never be dropped as a harmless 1: the sensor sets the limit, and a sensor that reads half the output makes the loop deliver twice the setpoint.

diagram.alt: Closed-loop gain y over r plotted against forward gain G from 0 to 40. With H equal to 1 the curve rises towards 1. With H equal to 0.5 it rises towards 2.
diagram.caption: As G grows, G/(1 + GH) approaches 1/H, so the feedback block alone sets the gain.

lead.text: Take a gain of 3 followed by an inner loop with forward gain 4 and feedback 0.5, all enclosed by a unity-feedback loop, one whose feedback gain H is 1. The inner loop is a feedback loop like any other, so it reduces to 4/(1 + 4 × 0.5) = 4/3, and the figure then shows a gain of 3 in series with 4/3, which multiply to 4.
The remaining diagram is a single block inside unity feedback, so its gain is 4/(1 + 4) = 0.8.

afterFigure.text: Reading the figure left to right, the pattern for any such diagram is to find a loop with no other loop inside it, replace it by its single gain, and repeat until no loops remain.

blocks.text: The feedback formula comes from e = r − Hy and y = Ge, and it changes to G/(1 − GH) if the junction adds, so the sign has to be read from the diagram. For large G the gain approaches 1/H, which is why the sensor's gain must always be kept in the calculation.

lessons.title: First-order response

blocks.text: A cup of coffee at 90 degrees in a room at 20 does not cool at a steady rate. It loses heat quickly while it is far hotter than the room, and ever more slowly as the gap closes, so that the temperature approaches 20 degrees without ever quite arriving. The same shape describes a capacitor charging through a resistor, a thermometer settling in a bath and a motor coming up to speed.

Each of these systems changes at a rate proportional to the distance it still has to go, and that one rule fixes the shape of the curve, leaving a single number, the time constant, to say how quickly the curve is followed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the step response of a first-order system from its time constant, find the time to reach a given fraction of the final value, and estimate the time constant from data.
intro.whyItMatters: Most simple sensors, heaters and circuits follow this response, and it is the building block of the loops that follow.

reveal.text: The next two screens write this rule as an equation and solve it, which is where the figure of 63.2 percent comes from.

lead.text: Pour a cup of coffee at 90 degrees into a room at 20 and it loses heat quickly at first and then more and more slowly, because the rate of cooling depends on how much hotter the cup is than the room. Newton's law of cooling says that the rate is proportional to this temperature gap.

In symbols, let y be the output, let its final value be Ku, where u is the input and K the gain, and let τ be a constant with units of time. Then the gap is Ku − y, and the statement is τ dy/dt = Ku − y. The rate of change is the gap divided by τ, so a large gap gives a steep slope and a small gap gives a shallow one.

afterFigure.text: The slope tracks the gap at every point, and that is all the equation says.

diagram.alt: A first-order step response drawn three times, with its tangent at t equal to 0, 1 and 2 time constants. The green bar is the gap to the final value and the orange line is the slope. The gap is 1.00, 0.37 and 0.14, and the slope equals the gap divided by the time constant each time.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to move along the curve. The slope is always the gap divided by τ, so it shrinks as the gap does.

lead.text: Starting from y = 0 with the input held at u, the solution of τ dy/dt = Ku − y is y = Ku(1 − e^(−t/τ)). Differentiating shows it: the slope is (Ku/τ)e^(−t/τ), and the gap Ku − y is Ku e^(−t/τ), which is τ times the slope, as the equation requires.

At t = τ the exponent is −1, and 1 − e^(−1) is 0.632, so the output has covered **63.2 percent** of the way to its final value. This is the reason τ is called the **time constant**: it is the time the system takes to cover 63.2 percent of the gap, and every further interval of τ removes the same fraction, 63.2 percent, of what is left.

afterFigure.text: The checkpoints follow from the same formula. After 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 time constants the response has reached 63.2, 86.5, 95.0, 98.2 and 99.3 percent.

diagram.alt: Three first-order step responses against time from 0 to 10 seconds, with time constants 0.5, 1 and 2 seconds. Each curve passes 63.2 percent of its final value at one time constant and 95 percent at three time constants.
diagram.caption: The curve keeps one shape. A larger τ stretches it along the time axis.

steps.headline: Find how long a sensor with τ = 8 s takes to reach 90 percent of its final reading.

workedSteps.text: The output is 90 percent of its final value when the gap has fallen to 10 percent, so 1 − e^(−t/8) = 0.9.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides. The exponential and the logarithm cancel.
Multiplying both sides by −8 gives the time, in seconds.
Two time constants are 16 s and three are 24 s, so 18.4 s falls between them, as 90 percent falls between 86.5 and 95.0.

steps.headline: Find how long the same sensor takes to reach 99 percent.

workedSteps.text: The gap has fallen to 1 percent, so e^(−t/8) = 0.01.
Take logarithms: ln 0.01 = −4.605.
Solving that for t gives the time in seconds.

reveal.text: At 1.5 time constants the response has covered 77.7 percent, between the 63.2 percent at one time constant and the 86.5 percent at two in the checkpoints listed with the figure.

lead.text: Since the gap is multiplied by e^(−t/τ), it shrinks at every instant and is never exactly zero, so the response has no moment at which it arrives. Engineers therefore define settling by a band around the final value: the response has settled when it enters the band and stays there, and the usual bands are 5 percent, which takes 3.0τ, and 2 percent, which takes 3.9τ.

The time constant must also be kept apart from a delay. A **delay** is a wait before anything happens, such as the time for a fluid to travel along a pipe, and it shifts the whole curve to the right without changing its shape, so the time constant is still measured from the moment the response begins to rise.

afterFigure.text: A response that has covered 95 percent is within 5 percent of its final value, which is why three time constants is the common estimate of the settling time.

diagram.alt: Two views of a first-order response. The first shows the same response with and without a 1.5 second delay, the delayed curve being the same shape shifted to the right. The second zooms in on the top of the curve and marks where it enters a 5 percent band, at 3.0 time constants, and a 2 percent band, at 3.9 time constants.
diagram.caption: A delay shifts the curve and leaves τ alone. The response only approaches its final value, so settling is defined by a band.

reveal.text: The tangent at the origin reaches the final value at t = τ, which is a quick way to read τ from a graph.

lead.text: A capacitor charged through a resistor follows the same equation. The voltage across the resistor is the gap between the source and the capacitor, so the current, and with it the rate at which the capacitor voltage rises, is proportional to that gap. The constant works out as τ = RC, and with R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 µF it is 10 000 × 0.0001 = 1 s.
Doubling either R or C doubles τ, which makes the circuit slower, since a larger resistance limits the current and a larger capacitance needs more charge.

afterFigure.text: Thermal systems behave in the same way, with thermal resistance and heat capacity taking the place of R and C.

diagram.alt: An RC circuit: a 1 volt step source drives a 10 kilohm resistor in series with a 100 microfarad capacitor, and the capacitor voltage v rises with a time constant equal to R times C, which is 1 second.
diagram.caption: In an RC circuit the time constant is the product of the resistance and the capacitance.

One reading at 63.2 percent fixes τ, and then every other time on the curve follows from the same formula.

recap.keyIdea: A first-order system closes the gap to its target at a rate proportional to the gap, so its step response is Ku(1 − e^(−t/τ)), which covers 63.2 percent of the way in one time constant τ.

blocks.text: The time to reach a fraction is τ times the logarithm of one over what remains: 2.3τ for 90 percent, 3.0τ for 95 percent and 4.6τ for 99 percent. The response never reaches its final value exactly, so settling is defined by a band, and a delay moves the curve without changing τ.
For an RC circuit τ = RC, and for any first-order system the tangent at the start reaches the final value at t = τ.

lessons.reviewLabel: A first-order plant in a loop

blocks.text: A first-order plant with a gain of 2 and a time constant of 10 s takes about 30 s to settle after a step, and in most applications nothing about the plant itself can be changed. Put a proportional controller round it, though, and the output no longer follows the plant's own equation, because the loop has a time constant and a final value of its own, and both depend on the controller's gain.
With a controller gain of 4 the loop's time constant is 10/9, or 1.11 s, so the same plant settles in about 3.3 s, while its output stops at 8/9 of the setpoint, about 11 percent short.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the closed-loop time constant and final value for proportional control of a first-order plant, and size the gain for an error limit.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows in one clean example what feedback does to speed and to accuracy, which the lessons on PID (proportional, integral and derivative) control build on.

steps.headline: Closing the loop on a lag

lead.text: The plant of the last lesson obeys τ dy/dt = −y + Ku, where u is the input. Suppose the controller is the simplest one possible, which multiplies the error by a constant: u = Kp(r − y), with Kp called the **proportional gain**.

Substituting into the plant equation gives τ dy/dt = −y + K Kp(r − y), and collecting the terms in y gives τ dy/dt = −(1 + K Kp)y + K Kp r. The product K Kp is the loop gain, as in the first lesson, and the equation has the same form as before, with a different coefficient in front of y.
For the plant used throughout, τ = 10 s and K = 2, so the loop gain is 2 Kp.

reveal.text: The next screen divides the equation through to see the new time constant.

lead.text: Dividing the equation through by 1 + K Kp puts it in the standard form τcl dy/dt = −y + Kcl r, where the closed-loop time constant is **τcl = τ/(1 + K Kp)** and the closed-loop gain is Kcl = K Kp/(1 + K Kp). Every result of the previous lesson now applies to the loop, with τcl in place of τ: 63.2 percent in one τcl, 95 percent in three.

The figure shows the plant with τ = 10 s and K = 2 under three gains. At Kp = 1 the loop gain is 2, so τcl = 3.33 s and the final value is 2/3. At Kp = 4 the loop gain is 8, τcl = 1.11 s and the final value is 8/9. At Kp = 16 the loop gain is 32, τcl = 0.30 s and the final value is 32/33, or 0.970.

afterFigure.text: Feedback has changed the plant's speed, which the plant's own parameters would suggest to be fixed. The same loop gain that sped the response up also set the final value just below the setpoint, and the two effects come together in the formulas.

diagram.alt: Closed-loop step responses of a first-order plant with time constant 10 seconds and gain 2, under proportional gains 1, 4 and 16. The time constant falls to 3.33, 1.11 and 0.30 seconds, and the final value rises to 0.667, 0.889 and 0.970, still below the setpoint of 1.
diagram.caption: Raising Kp makes the loop faster and lowers the final error, but the output stays below the setpoint.

steps.headline: For τ = 10 s, K = 2 and Kp = 3, find the closed-loop time constant, the final value and the error.

workedSteps.text: The loop gain is K times Kp.
The closed-loop time constant is τ divided by 1 + K Kp.
The final value for a unit step is the loop gain over 1 + K Kp.
The error is what is left of the setpoint, which is 1/(1 + K Kp).
The loop is 7 times faster than the plant and settles 14 percent below the target.
The loop gain is K times Kp.
The closed-loop time constant is τ divided by 1 + K Kp.
The final value and the error follow from the same loop gain.
The error left is smaller than the 14.3 percent left at Kp = 3.

reveal.text: The same division by 1 + K Kp changes the plant's own τ to the closed-loop value, whatever plant is used.

lead.text: The error 1 − K Kp/(1 + K Kp) simplifies to 1/(1 + K Kp), and the ratio of the closed-loop time constant to the plant's is τcl/τ = 1/(1 + K Kp), which is the same number. The figure plots it for K = 2: it falls steeply for small Kp and then flattens, so the first few units of gain buy the most.

Two limits are worth noticing. At large Kp the error shrinks without ever vanishing. Gain also has a limit set by the plant: a first-order lag cannot make the loop oscillate, yet a plant with a second lag or a delay in it can.

diagram.alt: A graph of 1 over one plus K times Kp against Kp, for K equal to 2. The curve falls steeply and flattens, passing 0.333 at Kp 1, 0.111 at Kp 4 and 0.030 at Kp 16. It is both the fraction of the setpoint left as error and the ratio of the closed-loop time constant to the plant's.
diagram.caption: One factor, 1/(1 + K Kp), is both the final error and the speed-up of the time constant.

reveal.text: Rearranging 1/(1 + K Kp) ≤ 0.05 gives K Kp ≥ 19, so the required loop gain is 19 and the required Kp is 9.5.

lead.text: A computer can step the loop equation forward in small time steps, a procedure called Euler's method. Each pass of the program computes the command u from the current y, and then moves y by 0.1 times its rate of change.

reveal.text: A simulation reaches the same destination as the formulas, and the exact response after 1 s, 0.527, is close to the Euler value.
The loop takes 1.15 s where the plant alone would take 11.5 s, ten times faster.

recap.keyIdea: Proportional control of a first-order plant gives a first-order loop with time constant τ/(1 + K Kp) and final value K Kp/(1 + K Kp), so more gain is faster and more accurate but never exact.

blocks.text: Substituting u = Kp(r − y) into τ dy/dt = −y + Ku and collecting terms puts the loop gain K Kp into both results. The error is 1/(1 + K Kp), which is also the ratio of the closed-loop time constant to the plant's, so the two improve together.
A simulation by Euler steps agrees with the formulas, and the remaining offset is what the next lessons set out to remove.

lessons.title: Second-order response

blocks.text: When a wheel drops off a kerb, the body of a car does not simply sink to its new height. It dips, rises a little past it and settles, and a car with worn dampers keeps bouncing for several seconds. The motion comes from a spring that stores energy, a mass that carries momentum, and a damper that takes the energy away, and the mass-spring-damper equation m x″ + c x′ + k x = F describes all three.
Of the three constants, two combinations decide everything about the response to a step: the natural frequency, which sets how fast it moves, and the damping ratio, which sets how much it overshoots.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the natural frequency and damping ratio of a mass-spring-damper, and from them the overshoot, peak time and settling time of its step response.
intro.whyItMatters: Most controlled systems with inertia respond in this way, and the numbers computed here become the specifications in the next lesson.

lead.text: A force F pushes a mass m, a spring of stiffness k pulls it back in proportion to its position x, and a damper of coefficient c resists it in proportion to its velocity. Newton's second law for the mass gives m x″ = F − k x − c x′, which is usually written as **m x″ + c x′ + k x = F**.

If the force is a steady push, the final position is found by setting the velocity and acceleration to zero, which leaves k x = F and x = F/k. How the mass gets there depends on the other two terms, and unlike the first-order system of the last two lessons it can go beyond F/k and come back, because the spring stores energy and the mass has momentum.

afterFigure.text: Two energy stores, the spring and the motion of the mass, are what make the equation second order.

diagram.alt: A mass attached to a wall by a spring of stiffness k and a damper of coefficient c, pushed by a force F. The position x is measured to the right.
diagram.caption: The mass-spring-damper. The spring pushes back in proportion to the stretch and the damper in proportion to the speed.

reveal.text: The damper is the only part that removes energy, which is why its size sets the shape of the response, as the next screen shows.

lead.text: Dividing the equation by m shows that only two combinations of the parameters matter. The **natural frequency** ωn = √(k/m) is the rate at which the mass would oscillate if there were no damper, and the **damping ratio** ζ = c/(2√(km)) compares the damper with the amount that would just prevent any oscillation. For m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m and c = 40 N s/m, ωn = √400 = 20 rad/s and ζ = 40/(2 × 40) = 0.5.

The value ζ = 1 is called **critical damping**, and it divides the responses into three kinds. For ζ < 1 the system is underdamped, so it overshoots and rings. At ζ = 1 it is critically damped and just fails to overshoot. For ζ > 1 it is overdamped and creeps towards the final value without overshoot, more slowly the larger ζ is.

diagram.alt: Step responses of a mass-spring-damper with natural frequency 20 radians per second, for damping ratios 0.2, 0.5, 1 and 2. At 0.2 the response overshoots by 53 percent and rings; at 0.5 it overshoots by 16 percent; at 1 it approaches the final value without overshoot; at 2 it is slower still.
diagram.caption: The same spring and mass with four dampers. Use the buttons to see each response, or all four together.

reveal.text: With half the damping the response is much more oscillatory, which the figure showed for ζ = 0.2 and ζ = 0.5.

lead.text: The height of the first peak above the final value, as a fraction of the step, is the **overshoot**, and for an underdamped second-order system it is Mp = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)). The formula contains ζ and nothing else, so two systems with different masses, springs and dampers overshoot by the same amount whenever their ζ is the same.
As ζ falls towards 0 the overshoot approaches 100 percent, which is the undamped oscillation. At ζ = 0.7 it is 4.6 percent, and at ζ = 1 it has gone.

afterFigure.text: The formula follows from the exact solution, in which the oscillation sits inside an exponentially decaying envelope. The peak falls half a period of the damped oscillation after the start, at tp = π/(ωn√(1 − ζ²)), and evaluating the envelope there gives the expression above.

diagram.alt: Peak overshoot in percent against damping ratio from 0 to 1. The curve falls from 100 percent at no damping through 52.7 percent at 0.2, 16.3 percent at 0.5 and 4.6 percent at 0.7 to zero at 1.
diagram.caption: Overshoot depends on ζ alone. Natural frequency does not enter the formula.

steps.headline: Find the overshoot and the peak time for the system with ωn = 20 rad/s and ζ = 0.5.

workedSteps.text: First compute the square root that appears in both formulas.
The exponent is minus π times ζ over that root.
The overshoot is the exponential of the exponent.
The peak time is π divided by ωn times the root.
The root is √(1 − 0.16).
The exponent is −π × 0.4/0.917.
The overshoot is e raised to that exponent.

lead.text: The oscillation of an underdamped response decays inside an envelope e^(−ζωn t), so the response stays inside a band of 2 percent about the final value once that envelope has fallen to about 2 percent, which happens at **ts ≈ 4/(ζωn)**. The settling time is therefore *longer* for the smaller ζ, which is the opposite of what the word damping might suggest to someone who thinks of it as slowing a motion down.

At ζ = 0.2 the formula gives 1.00 s and the response keeps ringing until then; at ζ = 0.5 it gives 0.40 s; at ζ = 0.7 it gives 0.29 s, because the ringing is mostly gone after the first peak. Natural frequency matters as well, since doubling it halves every one of these times.

afterFigure.text: Frequency alone does not describe the response: ωn sets the time scale and ζ sets its shape.

diagram.alt: Step responses with natural frequency 20 radians per second and damping ratios 0.2, 0.5 and 0.7, each with a band of 2 percent around the final value and a green line at the settling time 4 over zeta times omega n. The times are 1.00, 0.40 and 0.29 seconds. The less damped response takes longer to stay inside the band.
diagram.caption: Less damping makes the ringing last longer, so the response settles later.

reveal.text: With the damping halved from the example's 0.5 the settling time doubled, which is the reverse of the first-order rule.
The factor √(1 − ζ²) is the ratio of the damped frequency to the natural frequency, and it lengthens the peak time.

lead.text: Critical damping is sometimes taken as the ideal, but it is the ideal only if no overshoot at all can be tolerated, as in a door closer or a needle on a meter. Among all the dampers that give no overshoot it is the fastest, since a larger damper only slows the creep.

For many purposes a little overshoot is acceptable in exchange for a faster rise. The figure shows ζ = 0.707, which overshoots by 4.3 percent and reaches the final value sooner than the critically damped response. The damping ratio is therefore chosen to meet a specification.

afterFigure.text: The coefficient that gives critical damping is c = 2√(km). For the 2 kg, 800 N/m system this is 2 × 40 = 80 N s/m, twice the 40 N s/m of the example, whose ζ was 0.5.

diagram.alt: Step responses for damping ratios 0.707, 1 and 2. The 0.707 response rises fastest and overshoots by 4.3 percent. The critically damped response at 1 has no overshoot and is the fastest response that does not overshoot. The response at 2 is slower.
diagram.caption: Critical damping is the fastest response without overshoot. A little less damping rises sooner, at the cost of a small overshoot.

reveal.text: The fastest return without overshoot is critical damping, ζ = 1, which fixes c from the mass and the spring alone.

recap.keyIdea: A mass-spring-damper has natural frequency √(k/m) and damping ratio c/(2√(km)), and the overshoot exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) depends on ζ alone.

blocks.text: For m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m and c = 40 N s/m, ωn is 20 rad/s and ζ is 0.5, so the overshoot is 16.3 percent, the peak comes at 0.181 s and the response settles by about 0.4 s. Less damping means more overshoot and a longer ring, and ζ = 1 is the fastest response with none.
Doubling ωn halves all the times, while ζ sets the shape that those times are measured on.

lessons.title: Designing to a specification

blocks.text: A positioning stage might be specified to overshoot its target by no more than 10 percent and to settle within 2 seconds of a step. Both limits describe how the output looks on a graph, while a controller is designed with a damping ratio ζ and a natural frequency ωn, so before any design can begin the two descriptions have to be translated into each other.

The formulas of the last lesson already turn ζ and ωn into an overshoot, a peak time and a settling time, and run backwards they turn a written requirement into the smallest damping ratio and natural frequency that will meet it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to turn limits on overshoot, settling time and rise time into limits on ζ and ωn, and check a design against them.
intro.whyItMatters: It is how a written requirement becomes numbers a controller can be tuned to.

lead.text: The **rise time** is the time to go from 10 to 90 percent of the final value, the **overshoot** is the height of the first peak above the final value as a percentage of the step, and the **settling time** is the time after which the response stays within 2 percent of the final value. The **steady-state error** is the gap that remains at the end.

afterFigure.text: The settling band is 2 percent of the final value, not an extra 5 percent added to it. A response that rings between 0.97 and 1.03 has not yet settled, and one that stays between 0.99 and 1.01 has.

diagram.alt: A second-order step response with damping ratio 0.6 and natural frequency 3 radians per second. Marked are the rise time from 10 to 90 percent, the peak overshoot of 9.5 percent, the settling time into a 2 percent band, and the steady-state error, which is zero here.
diagram.caption: Four numbers describe a step response: rise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error.

reveal.text: The formula for overshoot has one parameter in it. The next screen turns it round to give a limit on ζ.

lead.text: The formula of the last lesson gives the overshoot from ζ. A designer needs the reverse, because the limit is on the overshoot and the unknown is ζ. Taking logarithms gives ln Mp = −πζ/√(1 − ζ²), and squaring and solving for ζ gives ζ = −ln Mp/√(π² + (ln Mp)²), where Mp is the allowed overshoot as a fraction.

A limit of 10 percent meets the curve at ζ = 0.591, and a limit of 5 percent meets it at ζ = 0.690. Since the curve falls as ζ rises, every larger ζ also meets the limit, so each overshoot limit becomes a *minimum* damping ratio.

afterFigure.text: The natural frequency appears nowhere in this calculation. A designer can therefore choose ζ from the overshoot limit and then use ωn to meet the timing limits.

diagram.alt: The overshoot curve against damping ratio, read backwards. A horizontal line at 10 percent meets the curve at a damping ratio of 0.591, and a line at 5 percent meets it at 0.690. Any larger damping ratio overshoots less.
diagram.caption: To read a limit on overshoot as a limit on ζ, find where the limit crosses the curve and take everything to the right.

steps.headline: Find the minimum damping ratio for an overshoot limit of 10 percent.

workedSteps.text: The allowed overshoot as a fraction is 0.10, and its natural logarithm is negative.
The quantity under the root is π² plus the square of that logarithm.
Divide the negative of the logarithm by the root.
Any damping ratio of 0.591 or more meets the limit.

steps.headline: Repeat for an overshoot limit of 15 percent.

workedSteps.text: The logarithm of 0.15 is −1.8971, and its square is 3.599.
The minimum damping ratio is the negative of the logarithm divided by that root.

lead.text: Settling is governed by the decay rate ζωn, as the last lesson found, so a limit of ts seconds requires ζωn ≥ 4/ts. The rise time is roughly 1.8/ωn for moderate damping, so a limit tr on the rise time requires ωn ≥ 1.8/tr. Both formulas are rules of thumb, and over the range of ζ between 0.4 and 0.8 they can be out by a quarter or more.

With an overshoot limit of 10 percent and a settling limit of 2 seconds, the first requires ζ ≥ 0.591 and the second requires ζωn ≥ 2, so ωn ≥ 2/ζ. The first view of the figure shades the pairs of ζ and ωn that satisfy both, and the second view shows the same limits as a region of the complex plane, where the **poles** of the system, at s = −ζωn ± jωn√(1 − ζ²), must lie to the left of −2 and inside a wedge about the negative real axis.

The rise-time limit applies to ωn alone, which is why it can conflict with a limit on how hard the actuator may be driven.

lead.text: Design A has ζ = 0.7 and ωn = 4 rad/s, so its overshoot is 4.6 percent and ζωn = 2.8 gives a settling time of about 1.4 s by the rule of thumb. It meets both limits.

Design B has ζ = 0.4 and ωn = 6 rad/s. Its ζωn is 2.4, so the rule gives a settling time of 1.7 s, which is within the limit, and it rises faster than A. It overshoots by 25.4 percent, however, and a response that is fast on every other measure still fails if it breaks one limit.

afterFigure.text: The specifications trade against one another, because a larger ωn means a faster response but also a more energetic actuator, and a larger ζ means less overshoot but a slower rise. The design is the point that satisfies every limit with the least effort.

Design B, damping ratio 0.4 and natural frequency 6, has 1.7 seconds but overshoots by 25.4 percent into the forbidden zone.
diagram.caption: The shaded band marks overshoot above 10 percent. The dashed vertical line is the 2 second limit.

reveal.text: A response at ζ = 0.45 overshoots by about twice the 10 percent that a typical specification allows, whatever ωn is, so only a larger damping ratio could bring it within that limit.
Overshoot fixed ζ at its minimum and settling then fixed ωn, which is the order in which the two limits are applied.

recap.keyIdea: An overshoot limit Mp fixes ζ ≥ −ln Mp/√(π² + (ln Mp)²), and a settling limit ts fixes ζωn ≥ 4/ts, so together they bound the damping ratio and natural frequency of a design.

blocks.text: For 10 percent overshoot the minimum ζ is 0.591, and for 5 percent it is 0.690. With ζ chosen, the settling limit gives the smallest ωn, and the rise-time estimate 1.8/ωn adds a second bound.
A fast design can still fail on overshoot, so each limit is checked separately.

lessons.title: Proportional control and droop

blocks.text: A thermostat that heats in proportion to how cold the room is will never quite bring the room to the dial setting. The reason is in its own rule: when the room is exactly at the setting, the error is zero and the heater, which has to replace the heat leaking through the walls, is told to do nothing. The room therefore settles a little below the setting, at the point where the error is large enough to command the power that the leakage requires.
This steady shortfall is called the offset, or steady-state error, of proportional control, and it follows from the control law itself, so a better heater or a better sensor would not remove it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the steady-state error of a proportionally controlled loop, find the gain that meets an error limit, and explain why an offset must remain.
intro.whyItMatters: Every use of proportional control meets this offset, and it motivates the integral term that follows.

reveal.text: The next screen shows why some error must remain, and the one after it gives the formula for the offset, from which the effect of Kp is read.

lead.text: The **proportional term** is u = Kp e: the controller's output is the error times a constant gain, and it depends on the error at this moment only, with no memory of what the error was earlier. This is the controller of the loops so far, and it is time to ask what it does when the plant has to be *held* at the target.

Take a heater and a room. To keep the room 20 °C above the outside air, the heater has to run continuously at whatever power balances the heat that leaks away, say 30 percent. Suppose the controller succeeded in making the error exactly zero. Then u = Kp × 0 = 0, the heater would be off, and the room would cool, which contradicts the assumption. The loop can only settle where the error is *not* zero, at a value that makes Kp e equal to the power needed.

afterFigure.text: A room that needs 30 percent power with Kp = 5 needs an error of 6 °C, and with Kp = 20 it needs 1.5 °C. The error falls as Kp rises, and it never reaches zero.

diagram.alt: The error a proportional controller needs in order to command the power the heater has to deliver to hold a temperature, plotted against Kp, for three rooms. A room that needs 10 percent power, 30 percent power or 60 percent power needs an error of power divided by Kp. The error falls as Kp rises but never reaches zero.
diagram.caption: The error needed is the holding power divided by Kp. A leakier room needs a larger error for the same Kp.

lead.text: The offset needed no model of the plant beyond its DC gain G0, the output per unit of input once everything has settled. At the end of the step response the output is y = G0 u and the controller gives u = Kp(r − y). Eliminating u gives y = G0 Kp(r − y), so y = G0 Kp r/(1 + G0 Kp), and the **steady-state error**, r − y, is r/(1 + G0 Kp).

The figure shows G0 = 5 with Kp = 1, 3 and 10. The loop gains are 5, 15 and 50, so the errors are 1/6, 1/16 and 1/51, or 0.1667, 0.0625 and 0.0196, and each response stops short of 1 by exactly that much.

afterFigure.text: Time plays no part in the formula, because the offset belongs to the end of the response and the dynamics only decide how fast it is reached.

diagram.alt: Closed-loop step responses of a plant with DC gain 5 under proportional gains 1, 3 and 10, and one with a load disturbance. The output stops below the setpoint of 1 by an offset of 0.1667, 0.0625 and 0.0196, and by 0.125 when a load of 0.2 pushes against the control.
diagram.caption: Each response stops short of the setpoint by an offset. A larger Kp shrinks the offset, and a load disturbance enlarges it.

steps.headline: Find the final value and the offset for G0 = 5 and Kp = 4.

workedSteps.text: The loop gain is G0 times Kp.
The final value is the loop gain over 1 + the loop gain.
The offset is what is missing from 1.
About 5 percent of the step is never delivered.
The loop gain is G0 times Kp.
The offset is 1 divided by 1 + the loop gain.
The final value is the setpoint less this offset, and it is closer to the setpoint than at Kp = 4.

reveal.text: Each tightening of the limit costs gain, and the next screen turns to what a large gain costs the rest of the loop.

lead.text: The loop of this lesson is a clean model, and real loops pay for gain in three ways. At the moment of a unit step the output is still zero, so the error is the full step and the command is Kp × 1: with Kp = 10 the actuator is told to deliver ten units, where the plant needs only r/G0 = 0.2 units to hold the new value. An actuator that cannot deliver ten units will **saturate**, staying pinned at its limit, and the loop's behaviour then differs from the linear one.

The same gain also multiplies measurement noise, since u = Kp(r − y) includes whatever the sensor adds to y, and in a plant with more than one lag a large gain will overshoot and eventually oscillate. The right gain is therefore the smallest one that meets the accuracy limit, and not the largest that the actuator tolerates.

afterFigure.text: A proportional controller has no memory of the error, so a small error that lasts for an hour is answered with the same small action as one that lasts a second. This is the source of the offset.

lead.text: A load such as an open window or a heavier payload pushes against the plant. If it acts at the input as a constant d, so that y = G0(u − d), then the equation of the loop becomes y = G0 Kp(r − y) − G0 d, and the output is y = (G0 Kp r − G0 d)/(1 + G0 Kp). The load lowers the final value by G0 d/(1 + G0 Kp), which is added to the offset that was already there.
With G0 = 5, Kp = 3 and d = 0.2 the output falls from 0.9375 to 0.875, and the last view of the offset figure earlier in the lesson shows the response stopping at that lower level.

reveal.text: The load took a further 0.071 from the output, and a larger Kp would reduce that shift as well as the original offset.
The controller is commanding about 33 percent power from the 3.3 °C error that remains, which matches the power the heater needs to hold 16.7 °C.

recap.keyIdea: Proportional control sends action in proportion to the present error, so a plant that needs a steady action leaves a steady error of 1/(1 + G0 Kp).

blocks.text: For G0 = 5 the error is 6.25 percent at Kp = 3 and 1.96 percent at Kp = 10, and meeting a 2 percent limit needs Kp of at least 9.8. A constant load adds to the offset, by the load's effect on the output divided by 1 + G0 Kp.
A larger gain reduces all of this at the cost of a harder initial kick and more amplified noise.

lessons.title: Integral action

blocks.text: A first-order plant of gain 2 under a proportional gain of 4 settles at 0.889 of its setpoint, because at that point the remaining error of 0.111, multiplied by the gain, is just enough to command the input the plant needs. A controller that acts only on the error of the moment cannot hold the plant at the setpoint itself, since there the error, and with it the command, would be zero.

Adding a second term that acts on the history of the error, with a gain of 0.8, brings the same plant to exactly 1.000, and every stable loop with this integral term reaches its setpoint in the same way.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute an integral term from a list of errors, explain why integral action removes the offset, and estimate how long a wound-up integral takes to unwind.
intro.whyItMatters: Integral action is in almost every industrial loop, and so is the windup it can cause.

reveal.text: A term that adds up a constant error keeps growing for as long as the error lasts. The next screen defines this term, and the screens after it show what that property does to the offset.

lead.text: Proportional control forgets. The **integral term** remembers: it is Ki times the area under the error curve from the start up to now, written Ki ∫e dt. The area grows while the error is positive, shrinks while it is negative, and stays put only when the error is zero.

On a computer the integral is a running sum. If the error is sampled every dt seconds, the term rises at each step by Ki × e × dt, which is the area of one rectangle times the gain. The rectangles have areas 0.50, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.05, the total is 1.0, and with Ki = 2 the integral term is 2.0.

diagram.alt: Four error samples of 1.0, 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1, half a second apart, drawn as rectangles with areas 0.50, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.05. The second view shows the running total of those areas, which reaches 1.0 after two seconds.
diagram.caption: The integral is the area under the error curve. The running total is the quantity the integral term multiplies by Ki.

reveal.text: The running sum is the memory of the controller, which proportional control lacks.

lead.text: The integral term changes at the rate Ki × e, so it can be constant only if e = 0. Suppose the loop has settled: every signal is constant, including the controller's output u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt, a proportional term plus an integral term, which is called **PI control**. The integral term is then constant, so the error is zero, and the output is whatever the plant needs. The proportional term contributes nothing at the end, since it is Kp × 0, and the integral term holds the whole of the control that the plant needs.

The figure follows a plant with gain 2 and time constant 10 s under Kp = 4. With no integral term the output stops at 0.889. With Ki = 0.8 it reaches 1.000, and the integral term, the warm line, climbs to 0.5, which is the input u = 1/2 that a plant of gain 2 needs in order to hold an output of 1. Raising Ki makes the approach quicker and adds overshoot, with a peak of 1.163 at Ki = 2 and 1.301 at Ki = 5.

afterFigure.text: A controller that must supply a standing action can do so through a standing integral, and then the error that Kp needs in order to supply it is zero.

diagram.alt: Step responses of a first-order plant with gain 2 and time constant 10 seconds under proportional gain 4 and four integral gains. With no integral term the output stops at 0.889. With Ki of 0.8, 2 and 5 it rises to 1.000, with peaks of 1.055, 1.163 and 1.301. The warm line is the integral term, which climbs to 0.5, the control the plant needs to hold an output of 1.
diagram.caption: The integral term keeps rising until the output reaches the setpoint, and it ends at the control that the plant needs. Larger Ki is quicker and overshoots more.

steps.headline: For a plant with gain K = 4 under PI control with Ki = 0.8, find the area under the error curve that the integral term holds when the output has settled at 1.

workedSteps.text: At rest the output is K times the input, so the input needed to hold an output of 1 follows from y = Ku.
At rest the error is zero, so the proportional term is zero and the integral term supplies all of u.
Divide by Ki to find the area.
The input needed is the same, 0.25, since the plant has not changed.
The integral term is Ki times the area under the error curve.
A larger Ki needs a smaller accumulated area to reach the same output, which is why the response is quicker.

lead.text: Integral action is not free. The controller now acts on the area under the error and so keeps pushing after the error has crossed zero, until enough negative error has cancelled the positive area. A larger Ki makes that push stronger.
The integral gain is therefore kept as small as the accuracy requirement allows.

diagram.alt: Peak overshoot of the PI loop plotted against the integral gain Ki, with Kp equal to 4. The overshoot rises from about 0 at small Ki to 5.5 percent at 0.8, 16.3 percent at 2 and 30 percent at 5.
diagram.caption: More integral action removes the offset sooner and costs overshoot.

lead.text: An actuator has limits: a valve cannot open beyond fully open, and a motor cannot exceed its rated current. Suppose a step in the setpoint is so large that the controller asks for more than the actuator can give. The output rises as fast as the limit allows, the error stays large, and the integral term keeps adding it up although the extra command has no effect. This is called **windup**.

The figure shows it in a plant with gain 2 whose command is limited to 1, so the output cannot pass 2.0, after a step to 1.8. Without protection the integral has grown so large when the output arrives that the controller keeps the actuator at its limit well past the setpoint, and the output climbs to 2.0 and settles only after about 98 seconds. If the integral is paused whenever the actuator is saturated and the error would push it further in, the output reaches 1.8 at about 24 seconds and stays.

afterFigure.text: If the error is 20 and the actuator is saturated for 10 s, the integral gains 200. When the output overshoots and the error becomes −10, it needs 20 s to unwind, and during all that time the actuator stays at its limit.

diagram.alt: Two runs of the same PI loop after a step to 1.8, with the actuator limited so that the output cannot pass 2.0. Without protection the output climbs to the limit of 2.0 and takes about 98 seconds to settle. With the integral paused during saturation it reaches 1.8 at about 24 seconds and stays.
diagram.caption: The integral term keeps growing while the actuator is at its limit. Pausing it during saturation removes the overshoot.

reveal.text: The unwinding takes longer than the winding up, because the error that unwinds it is smaller than the error that wound it up.

With zero error the proportional term is zero, so the integral term supplies the whole input. It settles at the value that holds the output and cancels the load, so the load leaves no steady error at all.

recap.keyIdea: The integral term is Ki times the area under the error so far, so a loop with integral action can settle only when the error is zero, and a wound-up integral costs time to unwind.

blocks.text: The integral term rises by Ki × e × dt at each step, and for the plant used here it ends at 0.5, the input needed to hold an output of 1. A larger Ki is quicker and overshoots more, with 5.5 percent at Ki = 0.8 and 16.3 percent at Ki = 2.
If the actuator saturates, the integral keeps growing, and stopping it while the output is clamped avoids the late overshoot.

lessons.reviewLabel: Derivative action and the full PID

blocks.text: A position servo under a proportional gain of 4 overshoots its target by 44 percent and rings for several cycles before it settles. Raising the gain would make it ring harder and lowering it would make it slower, so no setting of the proportional gain gives a response that is both quick and calm.

The third term of the PID controller acts on a quantity that the proportional and integral terms ignore, the slope of the error, which says where the output is heading. A slope term has a cost the other two lack, because a slope is large wherever a signal wiggles quickly, so it can turn a small amount of sensor noise into a large, rapidly changing command.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a PID output, explain how the derivative term damps a response, and estimate how much it amplifies noise.
intro.whyItMatters: PID is the controller in most industrial loops, and its derivative term is the one most often misused.

reveal.text: The slope term opposes speed, as friction does, which the next screen shows with the servo's step response.

lead.text: The **derivative term** is Kd de/dt, the gain times the rate at which the error is changing. When the output is racing towards the setpoint the error is falling fast, de/dt is a large negative number, and the term subtracts from the command, which acts like a brake that grows with speed. When the output is moving slowly the term is small, and when it is steady the term is zero, so it never changes where the loop settles.

The figure shows a servo with y″ + y′ = u under Kp = 4, with the derivative acting on the measurement. The loop's **characteristic equation**, the polynomial whose roots are its [[poles|The points s that set how a response grows, decays or rings. Met in 'Designing to a specification'.]], is s² + (1 + Kd)s + Kp = 0, so Kd adds directly to the damping, and ζ = (1 + Kd)/(2√Kp). With Kd = 0, ζ = 0.25 and the overshoot is 44 percent. With Kd = 1.5, ζ = 0.625 and the overshoot falls to 8 percent, and with Kd = 3 the loop is critically damped.

afterFigure.text: The derivative term is sometimes said to predict the error, but it extrapolates it linearly: it takes the slope of the moment and assumes it will continue. The term helps when the slope is a good guide to the next moment and misleads when it is not.

diagram.alt: Step responses of a position servo under proportional gain 4, with derivative gain 0, 1.5 and 3 acting on the measurement. With no derivative term the position overshoots by 44 percent and rings. With 1.5 it overshoots by 8 percent and with 3 it does not overshoot.
diagram.caption: The same proportional gain with three derivative gains. The derivative term acts as a brake that grows with speed.

steps.headline: Find the damping ratio for Kp = 4 and Kd = 2, and the resulting overshoot.

workedSteps.text: The loop's characteristic equation is s² + (1 + Kd)s + Kp = 0, so ζ is the coefficient of s over twice the square root of the constant term.
The overshoot formula uses √(1 − ζ²) = 0.661.
The exponent is −3.562, so the overshoot is the exponential of it.

steps.headline: Repeat for a stiffer loop, with Kp = 9 and Kd = 5.

workedSteps.text: The coefficient of s is 1 + Kd = 6, and the constant term is Kp = 9.
The damping ratio is the coefficient of s over twice the square root of the constant term.
The overshoot then follows from that damping ratio by the formula of the second-order lesson.

lead.text: The three terms add into a single command. The proportional term reacts to the error *now*, the integral term to the error accumulated so far, and the derivative term to the way the error is *changing*. A calculation with one set of values makes this concrete: with Kp = 2, Ki = 0.5 and Kd = 0.1, and an error of 1.5 whose accumulated area is 4 and whose slope is −3, the terms are 3, 2 and −0.3, and the command is u = 4.7.

Proportional control gives speed, the integral term removes the offset, and the derivative term adds damping, and a loop that needs only some of these leaves the others out. PI is the commonest combination, and PD is used where the plant itself has an integrator and no offset arises.

diagram.alt: A PID controller drawn as a block diagram. The error passes to three parallel blocks, proportional, integral and derivative, whose outputs add to form the command to the plant. In the first view the derivative block takes the error. In the second view it takes the measurement, and its output is subtracted.
diagram.caption: Three terms in parallel make the command. In the second view the derivative looks at the measurement, so a step in the setpoint does not produce a spike.

reveal.text: Each term is a gain times a different property of the error: its value, its area and its slope.

lead.text: The slope of a sine wave A sin(ωt) is Aω cos(ωt), so differentiating multiplies its amplitude by ω, which is 2π times the frequency in hertz. A noise of 0.01 at 50 Hz has ω = 314 rad/s and a slope of 3.14 per second, about three hundred times the size of the noise itself, and with Kd = 0.1 it adds 0.31 to the command. The proportional term would have passed the same noise through at 0.01 × Kp.

The figure plots the gain of each term against frequency on logarithmic axes. The proportional gain is a flat line at 2, the integral gain falls as Ki/ω, and the derivative gain rises as Kd ω, which at 50 Hz is 31. The second view shows the sum, which dips near ω = √(Ki/Kd) = 2.2 rad/s and then climbs in proportion to ω without limit.

afterFigure.text: Real noise is made of many frequencies, and the high ones dominate the derivative. That is why a derivative term that works well on a smooth simulation can make a real actuator chatter.

diagram.alt: Gain of each controller term against frequency on logarithmic axes, for Kp 2, Ki 0.5 and Kd 0.1. The proportional gain is flat, the integral gain falls with frequency and the derivative gain rises with it, reaching 31 at 50 hertz. The second view shows the sum, with and without a filter on the derivative.
diagram.caption: Derivative gain grows in proportion to frequency, so fast noise is amplified most. A filter caps it.

cases.label: PID with and without a filter

reveal.text: The slope is more than a hundred times the noise itself, and the controller would send this to the actuator multiplied by Kd.

lead.text: Practical controllers filter the derivative, replacing Kd s by Kd s/(1 + Tf s). At low frequency this is still Kd s, and at high frequency its gain levels off at Kd/Tf, so with Kd = 0.1 and Tf = 0.01 s no noise can be amplified by more than 10.

A second precaution concerns the setpoint. If the derivative acts on the error, a step in the setpoint makes the error jump, its slope is momentarily enormous, and the command spikes. Taking the derivative of the measurement, which cannot jump when the setpoint does, removes the spike and leaves the damping unchanged.

reveal.text: The filter caps the gain at 15, where the unfiltered term 0.3ω would reach 94 at 50 Hz and keep growing.

recap.keyIdea: The derivative term Kd de/dt brakes the approach to the setpoint and so lowers overshoot, and the full PID output is the sum Kp e + Ki ∫e + Kd de/dt.

blocks.text: For the servo with Kp = 4 the damping ratio is (1 + Kd)/(2√Kp), which rises from 0.25 at Kd = 0 to 1 at Kd = 3. The same term multiplies noise by its angular frequency, 3.14 per second for 0.01 at 50 Hz, so it is filtered and taken from the measurement.
Each term has a job: speed from the proportional term, no offset from the integral term and damping from the derivative term.

lessons.title: Stability

blocks.text: Here is the characteristic equation of a plant with three lags under a proportional gain K: s³ + 3s² + 2s + K = 0. With K = 4 the closed loop rings for a few cycles after a step and then settles, and its behaviour at any other gain is decided in the same way, by the three roots of this cubic and above all by the signs of their real parts.

James Clerk Maxwell used the same idea on steam-engine governors in 1868, in 'On Governors', the first mathematical analysis of the stability of a feedback device, and he showed that whether a governor settled or kept hunting could be read from the roots of its equation.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to relate the position of a root to the behaviour it produces, find the range of gain over which a cubic loop is stable, and say where it oscillates.
intro.whyItMatters: Stability is the first requirement of any loop, and the tuning rules that follow are built on its limit.

lead.text: After a disturbance, a loop that is left alone follows a combination of exponentials e^(st), one for each root s of its characteristic equation. A real root s = −1 gives e^(−t), which dies away smoothly. A complex pair s = σ ± jω gives e^(σt) cos(ωt), an oscillation of angular frequency ω inside an envelope e^(σt) that decays if the real part σ is negative and grows if it is positive.

The figure shows five positions in the complex plane beside the responses they produce. The loop is **stable** if every root lies to the left of the vertical line, where the real part is negative, since then every disturbance dies away. A single root on the right is enough to make a response grow.

afterFigure.text: Roots on the line itself, at ±2j in the third view, give an oscillation that neither grows nor decays, which is the boundary between the two behaviours.

diagram.alt: Five root positions in the complex plane, each beside the response it produces. A root at minus 1 gives a smooth decay. Roots at minus 1 plus or minus 3j give a decaying oscillation. Roots on the imaginary axis at plus or minus 2j give a steady oscillation. Roots at 0.3 plus or minus 3j give a growing oscillation, and a root at plus 1 gives runaway growth.
diagram.caption: Left of the vertical line the response dies away. On the line it neither grows nor decays. To the right it grows.

reveal.text: The real part of the root, −0.5, set the decay, and the imaginary part, 4 rad/s, set the ringing.

lead.text: For s² + as + b = 0 the roots are s = (−a ± √(a² − 4b))/2. If a and b are positive, a complex pair has real part −a/2, which is negative, and two real roots are both negative since their sum is −a and their product is b. If either coefficient is zero or negative, a root reaches the right half-plane or the line itself. For s² + 4s + 5 the roots are −2 ± j, so the loop is stable and rings at 1 rad/s.

For a quadratic the test is as simple as that, and it is the case behind the second-order lesson, since s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² has positive coefficients whenever ζ > 0. Cubics and higher need more than positivity.

reveal.text: A positive coefficient of s always gives a negative real part, so the loop is stable.

lead.text: Every coefficient of this cubic is positive for every positive K.

reveal.text: Positive coefficients are necessary for a cubic but no longer enough, as the next screen explains.

lead.text: Routh and Hurwitz found a test that avoids solving for the roots. For a cubic it says that the loop is stable if the coefficients a₂, a₁ and a₀ are positive and, in addition, a₂a₁ > a₀.

For s³ + 3s² + 2s + K we have a₂a₁ = 3 × 2 = 6, so the loop is stable for 0 < K < 6. The figure shows four gains. At K = 1 the roots are −2.33 and −0.34 ± 0.56j and the step response settles. At K = 4 they are −2.80 and −0.10 ± 1.19j, so the loop is still stable but rings for a long time. At K = 8 the real part of a pair has become +0.08, and the oscillation grows.

afterFigure.text: The growth at K = 8 is slow, which is how an instability often looks at first, and it is not always the steep rise that the word suggests. A loop can be stable for every gain below a limit, and the limit is the figure that matters.

diagram.alt: The loop with characteristic equation s cubed plus 3 s squared plus 2 s plus K, for four gains. At K equal to 1 the roots are in the left half and the step response settles. At 4 it settles with ringing. At 6 two roots sit on the imaginary axis at plus and minus 1.414j and the response rings steadily. At 8 two roots have crossed to the right and the oscillation grows.
diagram.caption: Raising K moves a pair of roots across the vertical line, and the step response changes from settling to ringing to growing.

steps.headline: Find the range of K for which s³ + 5s² + 3s + K = 0 is stable.

workedSteps.text: The coefficients are a₂ = 5, a₁ = 3 and a₀ = K, and they are positive when K > 0.
The second condition compares a₂a₁ with a₀.
The condition a₂a₁ > a₀ becomes 15 > K.
The loop is stable for 0 < K < 15, and the edge is the critical gain, 15.
The coefficients are a₂ = 4 and a₁ = 5, and positive when K > 0.
The second condition is a₂a₁ > K, so the edge of stability is where K equals a₂a₁.
The loop is stable for gains from zero up to that critical gain.

lead.text: At K = 6 the cubic factors as (s + 3)(s² + 2) = s³ + 3s² + 2s + 6. The roots are −3, which dies away, and ±j√2, which are on the vertical line. The loop rings steadily at ω = √2 = 1.414 rad/s, with a period of 2π/√2 = 4.44 s, which is called the ultimate period and is used again in the tuning lesson.

The figure shows the same fact in a form engineers use, the loop's gain and phase against frequency, where the phase is how far a sine wave that goes once round the loop is shifted in time, measured in degrees of a cycle. A signal travelling once round this loop at ω = 1.414 rad/s comes back with its phase shifted by −180°, which turns the subtraction at the junction into an addition, and with its size multiplied by K/6. If K/6 is below 1 the signal shrinks on each trip, at exactly 1 it repeats itself, and above 1 it grows.

diagram.alt: The loop gain of the plant K over s(s+1)(s+2), as a gain curve above a phase curve, both against frequency on a logarithmic axis. The phase passes minus 180 degrees at 1.414 radians per second, and the gain there is K over 6. For K equal to 6 the gain at that frequency is exactly 1, which is the borderline of stability.
diagram.caption: At the frequency where the phase reaches −180° the loop gain is K/6. When it reaches 1 the loop sustains its own oscillation.

reveal.text: The period is the quantity that the Ziegler–Nichols method in the next lesson measures by experiment.
Each plant has its own critical gain, and a large gain is not a safe default: this loop is stable only below 10.

recap.keyIdea: A loop is stable when every root of its characteristic equation has a negative real part, and for a cubic that means positive coefficients and a₂a₁ > a₀.

blocks.text: The real part of a root sets growth or decay and the imaginary part sets the ringing. For s³ + 3s² + 2s + K the loop is stable for 0 < K < 6, and at K = 6 the roots are −3 and ±j1.414, which gives a steady oscillation with a period of 4.44 s.
A stable plant does not guarantee a stable loop, because the lags in it can turn a high gain into an oscillation.
