lessons.title: Tuning a PID

blocks.text: Ziegler and Nichols published their tuning rules in 1942, at a time when process controllers had adjustable dials and the plants they controlled had no model to set the dials from. Their advice was to raise the proportional gain on the running loop until it oscillated steadily, write down the gain and the period, and read the other settings from a short table.

The rules still start many tuning sessions, and the numbers they give are best treated as a first guess. They aim at a lively loop, and applied to the loop of the last lesson they overshoot a setpoint step by 73 percent.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to set PID gains from the ultimate gain and period or from a step test, and judge and detune the result.
intro.whyItMatters: Rules of thumb are how most loops in practice are first set up.

lead.text: In 1942 John Ziegler and Nathaniel Nichols published rules that need no model, only an experiment on the loop itself. Switch off the integral and derivative terms, raise the proportional gain until the output oscillates steadily, neither growing nor decaying, and note two numbers: the **ultimate gain** Ku, which is that gain, and the **ultimate period** Tu, the time between peaks.

The loop of the last lesson, with plant s(s + 1)(s + 2), shows the experiment. At Kp = 6 it oscillates steadily with a period of 4.44 s, so Ku = 6 and Tu = 4.44 s, which the cubic test had already predicted.

afterFigure.text: On a real process the experiment is run carefully, with limits on the actuator, since the loop is at the edge of instability and a little more gain would make it grow.

diagram.alt: Step responses of the loop from the stability lesson under proportional control only. With Kp equal to 3 the output rings and settles. With Kp equal to 6 it oscillates steadily with a period of about 4.4 seconds, which makes 6 the ultimate gain Ku and the period the ultimate period Tu.
diagram.caption: Raise Kp until the oscillation neither grows nor decays. That gain is Ku, and the time between peaks is Tu.

reveal.text: The rule sets the working gain a little above half the gain at which the loop oscillates, which is what leaves a margin.

lead.text: The rules turn the two measured numbers into settings. For a PID controller written u = Kp[e + (1/Ti)∫e dt + Td de/dt], they are Kp = 0.6 Ku, an integral time Ti = Tu/2 and a derivative time Td = Tu/8. For PI the gain is 0.45 Ku and Ti = Tu/1.2, and for proportional control alone the gain is 0.5 Ku. The integral gain is Ki = Kp/Ti and the derivative gain is Kd = Kp Td.

With Ku = 6 and Tu = 4.44 s the PID settings are Kp = 3.6, Ti = 2.22 s and Td = 0.555 s. Ti and Td are times, and they are matched to the period of the oscillation that the loop itself produces: the integral acts on a time scale of half a period and the derivative looks ahead by an eighth of one.

steps.headline: Compute the Ziegler–Nichols PID settings for Ku = 10 and Tu = 3.7 s.

workedSteps.text: The proportional gain is 0.6 times the ultimate gain.
The integral time is half the ultimate period.
The derivative time is an eighth of the ultimate period.
In gain form Ki = Kp/Ti = 3.24 and Kd = Kp Td = 2.78.

steps.headline: Repeat for Ku = 8 and Tu = 3 s.

workedSteps.text: The proportional gain is 0.6 times Ku.
The integral time is half of Tu.
The derivative time comes from the ultimate period in the same way.

lead.text: The rules aim at a loop that rejects a disturbance quickly, with each swing about a quarter of the one before, and that is livelier than most applications want. For a step in the setpoint on this plant the figure shows an overshoot of 73 percent and a settling time of 14 s. Halving Kp and slowing the integral to Ti = 2Tu = 8.89 s brings the overshoot to 30 percent, at the cost of a longer settling time of 20 s.
The right response depends on the use. A level controller on a tank may tolerate a large swing if it settles fast, and a drug infusion may tolerate none.

diagram.alt: Step responses of the loop under Ziegler-Nichols PID settings, and under a detuned set with half the gain and a slower integral. The Ziegler-Nichols settings overshoot by 73 percent and settle in 14 seconds. The detuned settings overshoot by 30 percent and settle in 20 seconds.
diagram.caption: The rule gives a quick but lively loop. Detuning trades speed for a gentler response.

reveal.text: A PI controller is more cautious than a PID for the same loop, because it has the integral lag without the derivative damping.

lead.text: The experiment of the first method puts the loop at the edge of instability, which is not always allowed. The second method of Ziegler and Nichols, the **reaction curve**, needs only an open-loop step test. The output stays at zero for a delay L, then rises towards a final value K, and the line tangent to its steepest part reaches K after a further time T. For the plant in the figure K = 2, L = 4 s and T = 20 s.

With these numbers the PID rules are Kp = 1.2T/(KL), Ti = 2L and Td = 0.5L. Here Kp = 1.2 × 20/(2 × 4) = 3.0, Ti = 8 s and Td = 2 s. For PI the gain is 0.9T/(KL) = 2.25 and Ti = 3.33L = 13.3 s. The gain falls as the delay L grows, since a longer delay makes the loop oscillate at a lower gain.

diagram.alt: A step test on a plant: the output stays at zero for 4 seconds, then rises towards a final value of 2 with a time constant of 20 seconds. In the second view the tangent from the start of the rise reaches the final value after a further 20 seconds, which gives the delay L of 4 and the time T of 20.
diagram.caption: From a step test read the final value K, the delay L before the rise and the time T the tangent takes to reach K.

reveal.text: The delay is in the denominator, so the plants that wait longest get the smallest gains.

lead.text: Rules give a start, and the loop is finished by hand. The order matters. Set the integral and derivative terms to zero and raise Kp until the response is fast with only modest overshoot. Add the integral term next, enough to remove the offset in the time that the application allows, and raise it no further, since it adds lag. Add a little derivative last, if the response still rings, because that term is the one that amplifies noise.

Two cautions apply to a live process. Every experiment must keep the actuator inside its limits, and the controller needs a way to stop integrating while the actuator is saturated. Tuning the derivative first is the usual mistake, and it gives a loop that chatters on every wiggle of the sensor.

reveal.text: The same test gives gains for either controller, and a PI loop starts at three quarters of the PID gain.

recap.keyIdea: The ultimate-gain rules set Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Tu/2 and Td = Tu/8, and the reaction-curve rules set Kp = 1.2T/(KL), Ti = 2L and Td = 0.5L, as a starting point to be judged and detuned.

blocks.text: For Ku = 6 and Tu = 4.44 s the first set gives 3.6, 2.22 s and 0.555 s, and for K = 2, T = 20 s and L = 4 s the second gives 3.0, 8 s and 2 s. On the loop of the last lesson the first set overshoots by 73 percent, and halving the gain and slowing the integral brings it to 30 percent.
By hand, P is set first, then I, then a little D.

blocks.text: A controller on a real machine is a few lines of code run on a timer: every 0.04 s, say, it reads the sensor, computes a new command and holds that command until the next reading. The valve or motor it drives can deliver only so much, so a large command is sometimes clipped, and the plant's gain is usually known well enough to work out much of the command in advance instead of waiting for an error to build up.
None of these facts appears in the continuous equations of the earlier lessons, and each of them changes how a loop behaves.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose a sample time, write the discrete PID update, stop the integral at an actuator limit, and add a feedforward command.
intro.whyItMatters: These are the differences between a loop that works on paper and one that works on the bench.

reveal.text: The next screen shows the loop at four sample times, and the trouble starts well before the sample time reaches the plant's time constant.

lead.text: A computer reads the sensor, computes a command and writes it to the actuator once every Ts seconds, and holds the command until the next sample. A loop that was designed in continuous time therefore reaches the plant with a delay of up to one sample, and the delay matters when the gain is high. The figure uses a proportional gain of 5 on a plant with a time constant of 1 s. At Ts = 0.04 s the output rises smoothly to 0.833, and at 0.2 s it is still smooth.

At Ts = 0.3 s the output rings before settling, and at Ts = 0.5 s the loop is unstable. The reason is that a command computed from the error at one instant is held for a whole sample, during which the plant overshoots the target by more than the next sample can correct.

afterFigure.text: A common rule of thumb is to sample at least ten times in the rise time of the closed loop, which puts Ts at a tenth of the rise time or less. For this loop the rise time is 0.37 s, so the rule gives about 0.04 s, which is the smooth case.

At 0.2 seconds it is still smooth. At 0.3 seconds it rings and settles. At 0.5 seconds the sampled loop is unstable and the oscillation grows.

reveal.text: The rule is a guide for the longest sample time, and a shorter one is always safe, if more costly.

lead.text: At each sample the controller does the same short sequence of steps. The integral becomes a running sum, I = I + e × dt, and the derivative becomes a difference over one sample, D = (e − e_prev)/dt. The command is u = Kp e + Ki I + Kd D, exactly as in continuous time with these two substitutions.

The difference is a cruder estimate of the slope than a true derivative, and it is noisier, since it divides a small change in the error by a small dt. For this reason many controllers average several samples, or filter the measurement, before taking it.

afterFigure.text: The second view adds the part that real actuators need. The command is clamped to the actuator's range, and the integral is not allowed to grow while the command is clamped.

steps.headline: Run one sample of a PID with Kp = 2, Ki = 1, Kd = 0.1 and dt = 0.1 s. The error is 0.5, it was 0.4 at the last sample, and the integral was 1.0.

workedSteps.text: Add to the integral the error times dt.
The slope is the change in the error over dt.
Add the three terms.

steps.headline: Run the next sample, in which the error has fallen to 0.45.

workedSteps.text: The integral grows by 0.45 × 0.1.
The slope is now negative.
With I and D known, the command follows from the three gains.

lead.text: A valve cannot open beyond fully open, a heater cannot deliver more than its rating, and a motor has a current limit, so the command that the controller computes is clamped to the range the actuator can deliver. The controller must also know that it has been clamped. If the command is 140 and the valve delivers 100, the extra 40 does nothing, and an integral term that goes on adding the error is winding up in the sense of the integral lesson.

The simplest cure is the one in the second view of the discrete PID figure earlier in the lesson: when the command is clamped and the error would push it further out, do not add to the integral. The loop then comes out of saturation with an integral close to the value it needs, instead of one that has to be unwound.

reveal.text: The rule is sometimes called clamping, and it is the most common form of anti-windup. It blocks only the error that would push the command further past the limit, so the integral can still come down once the output passes the setpoint.

lead.text: Feedback acts only after an error has appeared. If something about the plant is known in advance, such as the input that holds a given output, the controller can supply it at once. This is **feedforward**: a command computed from the setpoint through a model of the plant, added to the output of the feedback controller. For a plant of DC gain 2 and a target of 6 the feedforward command is 6/2 = 3.

The figure uses a plant with gain 2 and time constant 10 s under Kp = 4. With feedback alone the output stops at 8/9 of the target, which is 5.33. With the feedforward command of 3 added, the feedback only has to correct an error of zero, and the output reaches 6.00. If the real gain is 20 percent lower than the model, the loop ends at 5.84, which is better than the 5.19 that feedback alone gives.

afterFigure.text: Feedforward does not replace feedback. It handles what the model knows, and feedback handles the rest, such as a wrong model and a disturbance that no model foresaw.

diagram.alt: Step responses to a target of 6 for a plant of gain 2 and time constant 10 seconds under a proportional gain of 4. With feedback alone the output stops at 5.33. With a feedforward command of 3 added, the output reaches 6.00. If the real plant gain is 20 percent lower than the model, the feedforward loop ends at 5.84 and feedback has removed most of the shortfall.
diagram.caption: Feedforward supplies the command the model says is needed, and feedback trims the rest.

reveal.text: The feedforward command is only as good as the gain it uses, which is why feedback stays in the loop.

lead.text: A loop that is correct in simulation still needs protection on a real machine. The command should be limited to a safe range even when the actuator could do more, and a timeout should force a safe output if the controller stops updating. A sensor that fails, by reading a constant or a value outside its physical range, should be detected and the loop moved to a safe state and not left to drive the output against its limit.
The derivative should be taken from a filtered measurement, and the sample time should be checked against the rise time of the tuned loop.

reveal.text: The output ends 0.21 below the target, against 0.86 below it for feedback alone, so a modest model error costs only a little.

recap.keyIdea: A working loop samples at a tenth of its rise time or faster, clamps the command and stops the integral while clamped, and adds a feedforward command so that feedback only trims the rest.

blocks.text: The discrete PID replaces the integral by a running sum and the derivative by a difference, and a loop computed too slowly can go unstable although its gains are unchanged. Feedforward from a model with the right DC gain brought a target of 6 to 6.00 where feedback alone stopped at 5.33, and with a 20 percent error in the model it still reached 5.84.
A loop also needs limits, timeouts and a safe action for a failed sensor.
